b085.name: the uridine stop signs, second try
b085.text: Side effects / stop signs: Stop if it makes you wired, numb, or weirdly irritable, and don't try to push through it. The most common problem people run into is the "choline headache", or a spaced-out kind of brain fog, which you won't find in the studies, but it's likely because UMP speeds up membrane synthesis, so if your choline availability is low, your brain can end up under-supplied. Other stop signs include insomnia, jitteriness and racing thoughts, irritability, going emotionally flat, or an upset stomach with nausea, cramps or loose stools.

E125: both lists are the protocol's (all eight stop signs; the post's "wired, numb, or weirdly irritable"), recorded, not cut

b086.name: the uridine psychedelic caution, second try
b086.text: Psychedelic caution: Don't take UMP on psychedelic days. If it makes your dreams vivid or suddenly lowers your tolerance, that's a sign your sensitivity is coming back, and the dose you're used to may be too strong now, so if you do take psychedelics later, go in assuming that, since chasing the old visual threshold can overshoot.
b086.why: "take that as a safety signal" said as what it means, in the article's own terms ("if sensitivity returns", W082): "that's a sign your sensitivity is coming back"; the dose line said as the person's ("the dose you're used to may be too strong now ... go in assuming that"); the label and "Don't take UMP on psychedelic days" kept (Codex called that line human)

b088.name: the 5-HTP "Who this is for", second try
b088.text: Who this is for: 5-HTP is not for every depressed person either. It could help, though, with a low-serotonin-looking pattern, where it's hard to fall asleep and your mood is low, without much warmth to it. At night you get anxious and keep going over the same things. It makes more sense if there's also a genetic or clinical reason to suspect a bottleneck in serotonin synthesis, like with Scott, whose genetic data pointed to a TPH2 bottleneck, and 5-HTP helped his sleep and mood. If you're already agitated, manic, on serotonergic meds, or using serotonergic psychedelics/entactogens, you shouldn't be casually experimenting with it.

b089.name: the 5-HTP tool, second try
b089.text: The tool: 5-HTP skips the step where your body turns tryptophan into 5-HTP, which makes it a more direct serotonin precursor. There's a broad review of 5-HTP that discusses where it fits in serotonin biology and what it's been used for (mood, anxiety, sleep, obesity, myoclonus), along with the serotonin-toxicity risk. People who respond to it can feel it quickly, because the mechanism is real, even though the evidence for depression and sleep is mixed, and weaker than people online make it sound.
b089.why: the uses after their category, in brackets ("what it's been used for (mood, ...)"), his list move; "discusses its role in" said as "discusses where it fits in"; the review's serotonin-toxicity side said as the risk it is (the first try's "its use ... in serotonin-toxicity cases" misread it: the review treats serotonin syndrome as a risk of 5-HTP, sections 8.2.1 and 9); the verdict turned round, the responders first and the evidence caveat last, without the "not as strong" tail (O9)

b090.name: Scott's 5-HTP and P5P, first try
b090.text: Scott took 100 mg 5-HTP sublingually at night, with 10–20 mg P5P sublingually in the morning. The P5P isn't there as a stimulant, but as the active form of B6, which the enzyme that turns 5-HTP into serotonin (aromatic amino-acid decarboxylase) needs. He's slow-COMT and sensitive to too much P5P, so the low dose matters, and more isn't better.

b091.name: the 5-HTP trial, first try
b091.text: If you're sensitive, start lower, with 50 mg 5-HTP at night for 2–3 nights, and go up to 100 mg only if the lower amount is clearly helpful and isn't activating. You can add 10–20 mg P5P in the morning, especially if the 5-HTP feels like it "almost works" but isn't converting cleanly. Don't combine the trial with other changes (like UMP, agmatine, D-serine, psychedelics, or medication changes). If it's the right tool, the first thing you'll usually notice is better sleep, a different dream tone, warmer mood, or less rumination at night.
